• Other names: Tadpole shrimp, Shield shrimp, Longtail tadpole shrimp, Rice tadpole shrimp, Triassic Triops, Dinosaur shrimp
  • Species commonly kept: Triops cancriformis and Triops longicaudatus
  • Optimal tank size: 20 litres
  • Keeping: easy; breeding: easy
  • Nitrate: less than 40 ppm
  • Diet: detritivore; predatory towards small organisms
  • Lifespan: 60–90 days
  • Colour: reddish-pink to brown

Triops kits are often sold as a system that needs no maintenance, but this is not true. Triops grow very fast, and adults need at least 1 litre of water each, optimally 4 litres; otherwise they may become aggressive and cannibalistic. Small containers get dirty very quickly, and sudden fluctuations in water parameters can kill the whole colony.

Kits are only suitable for hatching the eggs. Afterwards the Triops should be moved to a bigger tank.

Several varieties are on the market; the albino forms of Triops longicaudatus and Triops cancriformis are recommended for their look. The albino variant has a translucent carapace that becomes more opaque as it grows, and looks reddish-pink.
Triops has a cosmopolitan distribution; this small freshwater crustacean is widespread across Africa, Asia, South America, North America, Australia, Europe and the Pacific Islands.
They often inhabit rice fields, rain pools, ponds, swamps and other temporary freshwater bodies. Such habitats are flooded by rainfall and then dry out through evapotranspiration.
A 20-litre tank can house about 5–7 Triops, so that each adult gets 2–4 litres of water for an optimal population density.

Triops is a hardy, undemanding freshwater invertebrate, so care is relatively easy. Keep the water in excellent condition with partial water changes every few days, or at least weekly if there is no filtration: remove one-quarter (25%) of the water and replace it with fresh, dechlorinated water. This removes excess nitrate, which could harm them if allowed to accumulate.

Do not use tap water without letting it stand for a day or two (chlorine usually evaporates within 24 hours); it can harm the gills or even kill Triops.

Watch the eggs closely. As soon as they hatch, move the baby Triops to a separate tank to avoid predation by adults, and return them to the main tank when they reach about 2–3 cm.

Test the water weekly and keep temperature, pH and other parameters at ideal values. Triops tolerate a wide range of values but do not handle rapid fluctuations well. Keep a consistent feeding schedule, and acclimate Triops hatched in another container to the main tank's conditions before moving them.

Temperature: the ideal range is 22–30 °C. Above 34 °C most Triops species die off, and hatching of the eggs is also strongly affected when the water temperature goes beyond the recommended range.

pH: Triops are extremely hardy and tolerate pH 6.0–10.0, but the optimal range is 7.0–9.0.

Hardness: Triops can live in any type of water, but for the best results keep them in soft to moderately hard water so they thrive and breed successfully.

Lighting: adult Triops do not need high or intense light. They stay healthy under low to moderate light from any artificial source, such as normal fluorescent or LED aquarium lights. Light is essential in a breeding tank because the eggs can detect light and dark, and the hatching rate increases when lighting and temperature are favourable.

Substrate: Triops are bottom dwellers, so a considerable layer of substrate (about 5–7 cm) encourages their natural digging habit while searching for food. A deep substrate also improves the chance of recovering viable eggs, since many are buried out of reach of the adults. Suitable options are coral sand, aquarium gravel, small soft pebbles and aquarium sand. Sand is recommended as the most suitable, as it makes digging easier, causes less cloudiness and buffers the pH to the right level.

Filtration: a rearing tank needs no filter, as it is not safe for baby Triops; after hatching they are so small that they are easily sucked in even through a sponge pre-filter. A display tank also does not strictly need one, but then frequent water changes are required. For minimal maintenance some filtration is better, with no special requirements as long as the filter suits the tank size. Sponge filters are recommended for small Triops tanks: they are cheap, easy to maintain and clean, and offer plenty of surface for grazing.

Triops are omnivores and feed on animal and plant matter as well as commercial fish food. Suitable foods include:

  • daphnia
  • tubifex worms
  • grindal worms
  • bloodworms
  • detritus worms
  • fruit flies
  • copepods
  • brine shrimp
  • fish fry
  • insect larvae (preferably mosquito larvae)
  • fresh vegetables (boiled carrots, romaine lettuce, peas, potatoes, etc.)

In addition to these, high-quality foods such as shrimp pellets, shrimp granules, fish flakes and algae wafers can be given. Triops may also eat their shed skins, the foliage of aquarium plants (such as Elodea or Marimo moss balls), algae, detritus, biofilm and organic debris. If food is scarce, they can even filter food with their thoracic appendages.

Feed adequate portions at least twice daily and remove leftovers at the end of the day so they do not rot and spoil the water. Giving enough food keeps cannibalism to a minimum. As Triops grow, their diet becomes more predatory; studies showed that big animals eat significantly more animal prey than small ones.

Diet type: omnivore. Food preference: detritus and small organisms. Feeding frequency: 1–2 times a day.

Triops and live plants: it is not recommended to keep Triops in tanks with expensive plants. They are voracious and will eat any organic matter when hungry; soft leaves and roots are in direct danger. Unless the plants are fast-growing or expendable, do not keep Triops in planted tanks.

Triops are fun to watch because they are constantly moving in search of food. Although they are often found in large numbers in nature, they are not social animals. As they get bigger they become more predatory and even cannibalistic.

  • Social: no
  • Active: yes
  • Peaceful: yes (when young)

Tankmates: although highly opportunistic, Triops are not active hunters unless completely starving, so a peaceful community tank is technically possible.

  • Fish: do not keep with big or aggressive fish such as Botia lohachata, cichlids, loaches and goldfish. Tankmates should be calm, peaceful community fish (for example Panda Garra, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus).
  • Dwarf shrimp: not natural cohabitants, but they can be kept together. Triops will not touch healthy shrimp, but sick, injured or recently moulted shrimp can be eaten.
  • Freshwater snails: good companions; the only problem may be very small snails, which Triops will not let go once they have something that fits between their mandibles.
  • Crayfish and crabs: few problems with dwarf crayfish (such as Cambarellus diminutus) and small freshwater crabs (such as pom pom crab or Thai micro crab), which are too small to overpower Triops.
  • Dwarf frogs: adult Triops are too big to be swallowed and are safe, but small Triops will be eaten. African dwarf frogs will try to eat anything that fits in their mouth.

Triops reproduce in several ways. Sexually, when males and females are both present: the male inseminates the female, who lays batches of fertilized, desiccation-resistant eggs. Some populations consist of hermaphroditic individuals capable of selfing. Another method is parthenogenesis, in which an egg develops into an embryo without fertilization, so females can reproduce without mating. Eggs are released in batches of 10 to 100.

Females can modify their eggs according to conditions: when conditions are unfavourable they lay eggs with thick capsules that stay dormant until conditions improve. In a dry state the eggs can withstand temperatures up to 80 °C, can pass through the intestines of frogs or birds, and are easily carried by the wind, apparently even over very long distances. Because of this, Triops are widespread throughout the world.

Lifecycle: newly hatched Triops are tiny and orange, and develop through instars, each ending with a moult. Growth continues until maturity, usually one or two weeks after hatching, when they can breed and lay eggs. During long droughts the eggs stay in diapause, and hatch when the pool fills with rainwater. Under optimal conditions Triops grow very fast, almost doubling in size every day until they reach adult size.

Hatching the eggs:

  • Obtain viable dried Triops eggs from a local or online shop. They are often sold in kits containing dried eggs buried in coral sand, a plastic tank, food and instructions.
  • Use a clean, small, shallow plastic or glass container with water only 5–7 cm deep; do not use the main tank. Baby Triops have trouble finding food diluted in a large water volume, which reduces survival.
  • Use spring water, rainwater, or tap water treated with a dechlorinating agent or water conditioner.
  • Make a thin layer of sand in the container, then add the eggs and a little powdered food.
  • Avoid direct sunlight and keep the eggs warm under a lamp to stimulate hatching.

Eggs typically hatch within 48–96 hours under optimal conditions. Feeding can start 2 days after hatching.

Feeding baby Triops: give crushed fish food or spirulina powder until day 8, when they can be moved to the main tank after acclimation. Then switch to uncrushed flakes or pellets twice daily, and from the second week supplement with protein and vegetables.

Triops bury many eggs in the sand; these can be extracted from the substrate, dried and stored for later use. The eggs stay viable for many years; Triops longicaudatus eggs may remain in diapause for up to 20 years.

Eggs that do not hatch are the most common problem. Possible reasons:

  • An evolutionary defence mechanism: even under optimal conditions not all eggs hatch in a given hydroperiod; some stay dormant until later ones, spreading the reproductive risk over time.
  • Bad or wrong eggs: some kits contain too few Triops eggs, and most of the eggs are those of fairy shrimp, daphnia, etc.
  • Light: the eggs need light to trigger hatching, so use a very long light cycle during hatching, ideally 24 hours.
  • Temperature too low or too high: to hatch the eggs, keep the temperature at 22–27 °C.
  • Too many minerals: in nature, Triops live in pools that can dry out, and as they dry the dissolved minerals increase, signalling that the pool will soon be unsuitable. The eggs can detect this, so the fewer minerals and the fresher the water, the better.

Triops is a genus of small crustaceans in the order Notostraca. Some freshwater species are considered living fossils, with a record dating back to the late Carboniferous, over 300 million years ago. The name comes from the Greek tria ("three") and ops ("eye"), referring to the three eyes. Franz von Paula Schrank was the first author to use the genus name, in his 1803 work on the fauna of Bavaria. The genus has over 10 species; Triops cancriformis and Triops longicaudatus are the most common in the aquarium trade.

Classification: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Arthropoda, Class Branchiopoda, Order Notostraca, Family Triopsidae, Genus Triops.

Description: depending on species, they are typically 1–10 cm. Triops longicaudatus averages 1–4 cm in captivity and is reddish, brown or grayish-yellow. Triops cancriformis averages 6–7 cm, with a translucent carapace that becomes more opaque with time. They have a pair of dorsal compound eyes and a third eye (naupliar ocellus) between them, which can only distinguish light from dark. A broad shield-like carapace covers the upper body, followed by a long slender abdomen bearing two elongated appendages, resembling a tadpole. The body is divided into head, thorax and abdomen; the head bears two pairs of antennae, the anterior thorax has 11 segments each bearing a pair of appendages, and the posterior thorax has about 16–25 segments. Each ring may consist of up to 6 fused segments with up to 6 pairs of appendages used for sensing, feeding, locomotion and respiration. On the underside they have up to 70 pairs of legs, a number not seen in any other crustacean.

Lifespan: in nature Triops live just 50–90 days, or even less depending on water parameters and food availability.

Triops are sometimes used in the biological control of mosquitoes. They make an excellent pet for children thanks to their low maintenance and interesting lifecycle.
